versions.text:
Lune's starwort, a pale blue flower about the size of a thumbnail, grows only on the north slope of Corrow Ridge. For a decade its seed heads have come up nearly empty, a serious matter for a plant that lives only four or five years. What brought Ines Varga, an ecologist at Pellham University, up the ridge in 2023 was a 1988 photograph she came across in an old field guide, in which the slope is blue from the treeline to the crest.

Everyone at Corrow had an explanation. Petra Moss, the park's warden, blamed the late frosts, and so did Aldo Brisk, who has grazed his sheep on the slope for more than thirty years. Varga decided to test every idea at once. Her student, Tobin Hale, staked out twenty-five plots where the starwort still grew thickest. Some were fenced against the sheep, some sheltered under cloths on frosty nights, some watered in dry weeks, and some cleared of crowding grass. On the last set Hale did the bees' work himself with a paintbrush, dabbing pollen from flower to flower.

In September Ruth Callan, who teaches at the village school in Ottery, brought her pupils up to count seeds. One set of plots stood out: the flowers Hale had brushed held about forty seeds a head, against four or five everywhere else on the slope. The starwort, it turned out, was simply short of bees.

The board met a week later, and it was Moss who proposed the motion. She had blamed the frost for ten years, and she set that aside without a moment's fuss. The vote was unanimous, and the plan is simple: Hale will spend next July on the slope with his paintbrush, doing again what he did this year.

The grant will cover the cost of keeping him there, and it was found in a single meeting, on the strength of one summer's counting, by a board willing to hear that its own warden had been mistaken. Public bodies seldom move so quickly, or change course so gracefully. This July, for the first time in a decade, the starwort will have help in time.

In 2023 the park's warden, Petra Moss, asked Ines Varga, an ecologist at Pellham University, to find out why.

In September Ruth Callan, who teaches at the village school in Ottery, brought her pupils up to count seeds. One set of plots stood out: the fenced plots held about forty seeds a head, against four or five everywhere else on the slope. The sheep, it turned out, had been nipping off the flower heads before the seed could ripen.

The board met in October, beneath the 1988 photograph that hangs in its meeting room, in which sheep graze among the flowers. Its members pointed to the photograph, set aside a summer of counted seed, and voted to keep Brisk's flock on the slope. They adopted Moss's explanation instead: from June her wardens will truck water up the ridge twice a week.

The Ottery Courier, which sent a reporter to cover the vote, called the result a sensible compromise. It was nothing of the kind. A photograph records one afternoon in 1988; Callan's pupils counted every seed head on the slope. The watered plots ended the summer as empty as the rest. The board was shown what is harming the starwort, and it has chosen to spend its money on something else.

One set of plots stood out: the sheltered plots held about forty seeds a head, against four or five everywhere else on the slope. The board met in October. A frost is beyond the reach of any vote, so the board has turned to Varga: seed from the sheltered plots will go to her greenhouses at Pellham, where she will raise seedlings to be planted out on the slope each June.

The pupils will cover the two miles from Ottery on foot, and the school will count the walk toward their science course. Moss will record the seed counts each September and send them to Varga at Pellham. The board will review the arrangement after three summers.

Lune's starwort, a pale blue flower about the size of a thumbnail, grows only on the north slope of Corrow Ridge. For a decade its seed heads have come up nearly empty, a serious matter for a plant that lives only four or five years. In 2023 the park's warden, Petra Moss, asked Ines Varga, an ecologist at Pellham University, to find out why.

Everyone at Corrow had an explanation. Moss blamed the sheep; her proof was the 1988 photograph in her office, taken the summer before Aldo Brisk first drove his flock up: the slope blue to the crest. On the strength of it, the board has kept the flock off the slope until August since 2016. Brisk, who has grazed the slope for more than thirty years, blamed the late frosts. Varga decided to test every idea at once. Her student, Tobin Hale, staked out twenty-five plots where the starwort still grew thickest. Some were fenced against the sheep, some sheltered under cloths on frosty nights, some watered in dry weeks, and some cleared of crowding grass. On the last set Hale did the bees' work himself with a paintbrush, dabbing pollen from flower to flower.

In September Ruth Callan, who teaches at the village school in Ottery, brought her pupils up to count seeds. One set of plots stood out: the cleared plots held about forty seeds a head, against four or five everywhere else on the slope. The grass, it turned out, had grown tall enough to smother the starwort, because since 2016 nothing had grazed it in spring.

The board met in October and, having spent eight years keeping the sheep away to save the starwort, voted, amid some laughter, to bring them back to save the starwort. From next year Brisk will take his flock up in May.

Moss has kept the photograph on her wall, where it still shows what the board is hoping for: starwort enough to cover the slope again. Brisk has asked whether, in fairness, it might now hang in his kitchen instead. The minutes record the affair in a single solemn line.
